stem: When is P ⇒ Q false?
takeaway: Implication = a promise.
options: Only when P is true and Q is false

stem: 'If 2 + 2 = 5, then x > 3' is false because its premise is false.
solutionSteps: A false premise makes the implication VACUOUSLY TRUE.
takeaway: False premise → true implication.
why: A false premise makes the implication VACUOUSLY TRUE.

stem: Which is NOT a proposition?
takeaway: Questions and commands are not propositions.

stem: Match each term to its definition.
solutionSteps: Literal → an atomic sentence or a negated atomic sentence
Implication → P ⇒ Q, with premise P and conclusion Q
takeaway: Lecture 10 slide 11.
right: P ⇒ Q, with premise P and conclusion Q
a sentence that is always false
an atomic sentence or a negated atomic sentence

stem: P ⇔ Q is true whenever P and Q have the same truth value.
takeaway: Biconditional = necessary and sufficient.

stem: Select ALL correct statements about a knowledge base (Lecture 10). (Select ALL that apply.)
takeaway: KB + inference → action.
options: It must be written in natural language
It stores facts and rules as sentences in a representation language
An inference engine derives new knowledge from it
From P, P ⇒ Q, Q ⇒ R we can infer R

stem: A formal language's grammar defines ______ and its semantic rules define ______.
takeaway: Syntax vs semantics.
options: the syntax of legal sentences; their meaning

stem: Which sentence is equivalent to P ⇒ Q?
takeaway: Contraposition.

stem: Match each equivalence to its name.
solutionSteps: α ∨ (β ∧ γ) ≡ (α ∨ β) ∧ (α ∨ γ) → distributivity of ∨ over ∧
takeaway: Equivalence table.
Flip the operator.

stem: Which FOL sentence says 'every king is a person'?
takeaway: ∀ pairs with ⇒.

whyWrong.D: Says everything is a king and a person.

stem: ∀x ∃y Loves(x, y) means the same as ∃y ∀x Loves(x, y).
solutionSteps: Order matters: 'everyone loves someone' vs 'someone is loved by everyone'.
takeaway: Quantifier order.
why: Order matters: 'everyone loves someone' vs 'someone is loved by everyone'.

stem: Match each FOL expression to its category.
solutionSteps: Father(John) → function applied to a term (names an object)
takeaway: Term names an object; predicate is true/false.
right: function applied to a term (names an object)

stem: By De Morgan for quantifiers, 'All cats do not talk' (∀x ¬P(x)) is equivalent to…
takeaway: ∀x ¬P ⇔ ¬∃x P.
options: There exists a cat that talks
There does not exist a cat that talks (¬∃x P(x))

stem: In Existential Instantiation, what must the replacement constant be?
takeaway: Fresh constant names an unspecified existing object.
options: A new constant that does not appear elsewhere in the KB

stem: Select ALL steps of FOL inference by propositionalisation. (Select ALL that apply.)
takeaway: EI → UI → propositionalise → infer.
options: Apply Existential Instantiation with fresh constants
Run a complete propositional inference method
Apply Universal Instantiation to create ground instances

stem: Propositionalisation can be impractical because it may generate very many ground instances, especially with functions or large domains.
takeaway: Practical limitation.

stem: Match each reasoning/inference type to its example.
solutionSteps: Deductive reasoning → All students must submit; Mia is a student → Mia must submit
Inductive reasoning → Last five lab-goers passed; Leo attends → Leo will probably pass
Machine learning inference → Trained flower classifier predicts Iris setosa for new measurements
takeaway: Deduction certain; induction probable.
right: Assume the opposite and find a contradiction
Last five lab-goers passed; Leo attends → Leo will probably pass
All students must submit; Mia is a student → Mia must submit

stem: Deductive conclusions are certain if the premises are true, while inductive conclusions are only probable.
takeaway: Key difference.

stem: KB ⊨ γ holds when…
takeaway: No KB-true model makes γ false.
options: γ is true in at least one model of KB
KB and γ have the same symbols
γ is true in every model in which KB is true
KB is true in every model of γ

stem: Rain example: KB = P ∧ (P ⇒ Q). In how many of the 4 models is KB true, and is Q true in them? (number, Yes/No)
takeaway: Only model 1 (P = T, Q = T).

stem: Select ALL steps of model checking in order. (Select ALL that apply.)
takeaway: List → generate → filter → check.
options: Check the query in those models

stem: From P and P ⇒ Q we derive Q. This inference rule is…
takeaway: Theorem proving.

stem: Theorem proving needs to enumerate all possible models.

why: Theorem proving builds a proof chain WITHOUT enumerating all models.

stem: To prove KB ⊨ γ by contradiction, which sentence do we show is unsatisfiable?
takeaway: Negate only the query.

stem: Deriving the empty clause □ by resolution proves that the starting clause set is satisfiable.
solutionSteps: □ proves the set is UNSATISFIABLE (a contradiction).

why: □ proves the set is UNSATISFIABLE (a contradiction).

stem: Resolving clauses (P ∨ Q) and (¬P ∨ R) gives the resolvent ______.

stem: Which is in conjunctive normal form (CNF)?
takeaway: CNF = AND of ORs of literals.

stem: P ∧ ¬P is unsatisfiable.

stem: Facts and rules are stored as sentences in a knowledge ______.

stem: A model in propositional logic is…

a truth table of all sentences

stem: Which sentence says 'Some student is enrolled in AI'?

stem: Machine learning inference means a trained model uses new input to produce a prediction.

stem: Reasoning where a pattern in observations supports a likely (probable) conclusion is called ______ reasoning.

stem: And-elimination lets us infer α from α ∧ β.

stem: Replacing a universally quantified variable with a ground term is called Universal ______.
takeaway: UI.

stem: UI may be applied repeatedly with different ground terms to generate multiple consequences, while EI is applied once to an existential sentence.
takeaway: UI many times; EI once with a fresh constant.

subtopic: Evaluate a sentence in a model
stem: In the model P = T, Q = T, R = T, the sentence (Q ⇔ R) ⇒ R is true.

stem: KB = { R ⇒ P , ¬R ∨ ¬R }. Query γ = P ∧ R. By model checking over P, Q, R: (1) in how many of the 8 models is KB true? (2) Does KB ⊨ γ? (Yes/No)
solutionSteps: Some KB-true model makes γ false → KB does not entail γ.
takeaway: KB ⊨ γ iff M(KB) ⊆ M(γ): no model where KB is true and γ is false.

stem: KB = { R , R ⇔ P }. Query γ = R ∨ R. By model checking over P, Q, R: (1) in how many of the 8 models is KB true? (2) Does KB ⊨ γ? (Yes/No)

takeaway: KB ⊨ γ iff M(KB) ⊆ M(γ): no model where KB is true and γ is false.

stem: Resolve the clauses (R ∨ ¬P) and (¬R ∨ Q). What is the resolvent?
